TASK: CHECK EACH SENTENCE AGAINST THE CLAIMS

You are an adversarial fact checker. Your job is to find every sentence below that says something the CLAIMS do not support. Do not pass a sentence to be agreeable and do not fail one to look diligent. A sentence may read as confident or well written; that is evidence about its writer, not about the claims.

Label every sentence with exactly one of:
- "supported": every factual part of the sentence (each number, each name, each count, each comparison, each cause, each "most", "all", "only" or "none") is stated by one or more of the claims, or follows from them directly with no new number. Give the ids of the claims that together support it.
- "unsupported": any factual part is not stated by the claims, contradicts them, changes a number, drops a qualification a claim carries ("at most", "a bound", "notional", "not established", "candidate"), or states a number no claim states. Say which part, in the reason.
- "no_factual_content": the sentence states nothing that could be true or false about the world: a transition, a statement of what the section will do, a definition of a word the report uses.

The NAMES table maps a code in a claim to the name a sentence uses; a sentence that uses the name is read as if it used the code. A sentence that names a statistical body is checked against the claims for that body.

Return ONLY a JSON array, one object per sentence, in order, with no prose before or after it and no code fence:

B2: the check for definitions surface (Concept/term definitions published, versioned, linked from variables)
B4: the check for quality metadata (Data-quality attributes (error measures, suppression rules, revisions policy) published as metadata, not prose)
D3: the check for provenance completeness (Source lineage published (collection → processing → product))
D4: the check for no dark data (Statutory products enumerable from a public inventory (data.gov/agency inventory current))
G4: the check for authority metadata (The issuing authority of a data product is carried as machine-readable metadata on the product's catalog record: in `publisher`, the field DCAT-US 3.0 defines for it (Recommended), or in the agency codes DCAT-US 1.1 requires of federal datasets (`bureauCode`, `programCode`), which DCAT-US 3.0 does not define and does not reject)

SENTENCES
S1: The same distinction between an error and a failure bounds the measurement as a whole, because a refused request shows only that the scanner was not served, not that the thing it sought is missing.
S2: For example, 20 of the Census Bureau's findings, spread over the tests of variable-level semantics, quality metadata, provenance completeness, no dark data and authority metadata, are errors and not failures.
S3: They are errors because no record among the 1,810 in the catalog that census.gov serves names the probed product, and the department's inventory, which the indicator also names, refused the request and could not be read, so although the body's organization on catalog.data.gov was read, absence is not established.
S4: More broadly, the scanner, which identified itself and did not log in, met a refusal by the host or a disallow in robots.txt on 24 of the 89 findings for that body.
S5: Among its 27 absences, moreover, 4 were judged only after some refused or disallowed probes had been set aside, so those verdicts rest on only part of the evidence.
S6: Access also bounds which bodies the comparison can include, since of the 16 statistical bodies in the measurement only 13 are ranked.
S7: The three left out, which section 3 named, have no scored test with a judged row.
S8: A body's place in the ranking can rest on far less evidence than its full set of findings would suggest.
S9: As section 4 explained, the published matrices carry one row per test and surface, and on them the Census Bureau has 18 failing of 39 judged rows.
S10: Under the hierarchical equal-weight score, however, the Bureau ranks 7 of 13 with a score of 0.143, and that position turns on a single test, whether concept definitions are published, versioned and linked from variables, on which 0 of 2 judged rows passed.
S11: Were that one verdict reversed, the Bureau would rank 1, so a reader should take a body's place as a statement about a few tests rather than about its readiness as a whole.
S12: The framework is also larger than the part of it this measurement scored.
S13: Two further indicators, for access policy coherence and for discoverability from the product page, are candidates, and a candidate enters no framework count until the operator adopts it.
S14: Of the framework's 48 indicators, as section 2 reported, 23 have been measured and 24 are specified only.
S15: What holds back the 25 indicators not yet counted as measured differs by kind: 11 have no standard to measure against, 7 need the cooperation of agencies, 6 need open tooling, 1 is not blocked at all, and none is blocked by funding, so money is not what stands between these indicators and their measurement.
S16: Finally, only part of the framework's evidence can be traced to an exact place in a source.
S17: Of 50 indicator evidence cells, 10 carry a pinpoint locator, and of the 154 links that tie an indicator to its evidence, 34 point at a located document.
S18: Moreover, 16 indicators have no such link at all, and 84 of the 282 documents admitted to the record are cited through one.
S19: A reader can therefore confirm that a source stands behind much of the framework, but can find the exact passage behind an indicator in only 10 cases.
